Disaggregation Modeling in R with INLA: Spatial, Multivariate, and Spatio-Temporal Models

Fernando Rodriguez Avellaneda

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
fernando.rodriguezavellaneda@kaust.edu.sa

Paula Moraga

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
paula.moraga@kaust.edu.sa

2026-02-02

Abstract

Reliable high-resolution data is often unavailable due to privacy constraints or the high cost of fine-scale sampling, leaving researchers with data aggregated over coarse administrative units. Spatial disaggregation is essential for overcoming this limitation, as it enhances spatial resolution to uncover hidden local patterns and enables policymakers to make more precise, evidence-based decisions. We propose a robust spatial disaggregation framework and extend it to multivariate and spatio-temporal settings. Our approach assumes the existence of an underlying latent Gaussian field that represents the true process at a fine scale; by linking this latent field to the aggregated response variables, we can integrate high-resolution covariates for explanatory purposes. Leveraging the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) in R, our models provide a computationally efficient alternative to traditional MCMC methods, allowing for sophisticated uncertainty quantification across complex spatial and temporal dimensions.

1 Introduction

2 Methodology

3 Spatial disaggregation of PM2.5 concentration

In this section, we illustrate spatial disaggregation by improving the resolution of PM2.5 concentrations in Portugal from 10km to 2km. We used annual air quality reanalysis data for Portugal provided by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (Inness et al. 2019), a high-resolution product developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). This publicly accessible dataset, available at https://ads.atmosphere.copernicus.eu/datasets/cams-europe-air-quality-reanalyses, integrates satellite observations and auxiliary information to get estimations of air pollution levels in a very corase resolution.

3.1 Data acquisition and preprocessing

To download the data, you need to create an account on the Atmospheric Data Store (ADS), accept the terms and conditions, and obtain the “Licence to use Copernicus Products.” After setup, the data can be downloaded using the Python API. More details on setting up the API are available at https://ads.atmosphere.copernicus.eu/how-to-api. In our request, the argument \(\texttt{variable = ["particulate_matter_2.5um"]}\) selects PM2.5 concentrations, \(\texttt{model = ["ensemble"]}\) specifies the ensemble product, \(\texttt{level = ["0"]}\) indicates the surface level, \(\texttt{type = ["validated_reanalysis"]}\) requests the validated reanalysis product, and \(\texttt{year = ["2022"]}\) and \(\texttt{month = ["01"]}\) restrict the download to January 2022.

After downloading and unzipping the data, we use the terra package to read the \(\texttt{nc}\) file. NetCDF (Network Common Data Form) files are widely used for storing multi-dimensional scientific data, such as climate or GIS datasets, because they are self-describing, portable, and efficient for large arrays. The original dataset contains hourly samples for the 31 days of January 2022, totaling 744 observations. Since our focus is on identifying mean trends, we calculated the average PM2.5 concentration for each location. As the original data covers the entire European continent, we cropped the spatial extent to focus specifically on Portugal. To provide better geographical context in our visualizations, we also included the administrative boundaries of Portugal and Spain for clear regional identification using packages rnaturalearth and sf. Finally for plotting we used ggplot2, tidyterra and viridis packages.

To simplify replication and avoid the ADS download and NetCDF preprocessing steps, we provide the preprocessed dataset as \(\texttt{pm2p5.csv}\), which contains the processed PM2.5 values in CSV format.

# Define the squared study region and convert to dataframe
sq <- ext(-9.7,-6,36.9,42.3)

# Read the dataset and compute mean value (From source)
r <- rast("../../../../data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm2p5.l0.2022-01.nc")
r_mean <- app(r, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq <- crop(r_mean, sq)
df <- as.data.frame(r_sq, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
df <- df[order(df$y,df$x), ]
names(df) <- c("longitude","latitude","pm2p5")
write.csv(df, "../../../../data/pm2p5.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Read dataset from preprocess file 
df <- read.csv("../../../../data/pm2p5.csv")
 
# Get portugal and Spain borders
boundary <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("Portugal","Spain")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot PM2.5 contamination and boundary countries
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

Figure 3.1: Mean PM2.5 concentration in Portugal during January 2022. Country boundaries for Portugal and Spain are overlaid for geographic reference.

Figure (3.1) shows the spatial distribution of mean PM2.5 over the Portugal for January 2022. Higher concentrations are observed in northern Portugal. The map is provided on the original CAMS grid (about 0.1\(^\circ\), roughly 10 km), which is relatively coarse for local-scale interpretation; we therefore target a finer resolution of 0.02\(^\circ\) (approximately 2 km) using spatial disaggregation.

3.2 Input grid, spatial mesh, and prediction locations

The first step in the disaggregation workflow is to construct an input grid that matches the support of the observed data. Using the dataframe \(\texttt{df}\), we build a squared grid as an \(\texttt{sf}\) object with the same spatial extent and dimensions as the original dataset. The second step is to build a spatial mesh that is finer than the initial resolution of the data, as shown on the right side of Figure (3.2). This panel displays a portion of the triangulated mesh, represented by black segments, together with the original gridded support, shown in red. Finally, to achieve the target disaggregation from 0.1\(^\circ\) to 0.02\(^\circ\), we define the prediction points on the desired high resolution grid. The variable \(\texttt{spf}\) controls the disaggregation factor. Specifically, setting \(\texttt{spf}=5\) increases the resolution within each original cell by a factor of \(5 \times 5 = 25\), as illustrated on the left side of Figure (3.2), where red lines denote the original grid and blue dots indicate the prediction locations under the disaggregated scenario.

# Initial squared grid 
map <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(df$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df$latitude)))))
st_geometry(map) <- "geometry"
st_crs(map) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Spatial mesh 

sq_sf <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(sq))

hexpts <- fm_hexagon_lattice(
  bnd = st_buffer(sq_sf, 0.1), 
  edge_len = 0.05
)

mesh <- fm_mesh_2d(
  loc = hexpts,
  max.edge = 0.1,
  offset = 0.05
)

# prediction points

spf <- 5 # spatial factor
def <- abs(unique(df$latitude)[2]-unique(df$latitude)[1])/2 

x <- seq(min(df$longitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(df$longitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(df$longitude))*spf)

y <- seq(min(df$latitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(df$latitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(df$latitude))*spf)

dp <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))
dpdf <- data.frame(dp)
names(dpdf) <- c("x","y")

dpdf_sf <- st_as_sf(dpdf,coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")
dpdf_sf$id <- 1:nrow(dpdf)

# Plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), pty = "s")
plot(mesh,xlim = c(-9.65,-9.45),ylim = c(36.5,37.5))
plot(map$geometry, add = TRUE, border = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(map$geometry, border = "red", lwd = 2 ,xlim = c(-9.7,-9.5),ylim = c(36.9,37.1))
plot(dpdf_sf$geometry, add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 1)

Figure 3.2: Spatial discretization for disaggregation. Original grid support is shown in red. Prediction points for $ exttt{spf}=5$ are shown in blue (left), and a portion of the triangulated mesh is shown in black (right)

3.3 Covariates

We incorporate high resolution elevation data, at approximately \(60\)m resolution, from the EuroDEM product maintained by EuroGeographics (EuroGeographics and European NMCAs 2023) that is available in the following website https://www.mapsforeurope.org/datasets/euro-dem. Elevation is included as a covariate to relate PM2.5 concentrations with changes in altitude and to improve the explanatory power of the spatial disaggregation model across the study region. To use this covariate within the disaggregation framework, we align its spatial support with both the original CAMS grid and the high resolution prediction grid, by aggregating elevation to the 0.1\(^\circ\) input cells and extracting values at the 0.02\(^\circ\) prediction locations. Figure (3.3) illustrates the resulting elevation focused on Portugal, on the input grid, shown on the left, and at the prediction points, shown on the right. This step can be computationally demanding because EuroDEM is provided at very fine resolution and covers all of Europe, and it must be reprojected to EPSG:4326 before cropping. To reduce computation time, we provide a preprocessed version already reprojected, aggregated and cropped to the study region called \(\texttt{eurodemc.tif}\).

# Time consuming: This preprocessing takes roughly 40 minutes to be executed
# r <- rast("../../../../data/eurodem.tif")
# r_map <- project(r, "EPSG:4326")
# writeRaster(r_map, "../../../../data/eurodemp.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
# r_map <- rast("../../../../data/eurodemp.tif")
# r_crop <- crop(r_map,sq_sf)
# r_ag <- aggregate(r_crop, fact = 2, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
# writeRaster(r_ag, "../../../../data/eurodemc.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

# Time consuming: after preprocessing this part takes around 1 minute to be executed
r_crop <- rast("../../../../data/eurodemc.tif")

# Extract elevation values in the original dataset
map$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map,mean,na.rm = TRUE)$eurodem
map$elev[is.nan(map$elev)] <- 0

# Create the prediction dataset in sf format
map_pred <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(df$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df$latitude)))*spf))
st_crs(map_pred) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Extract elevation values in the prediction dataset
map_pred$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map_pred,mean,na.rm = TRUE)$eurodem
map_pred$elev[is.nan(map_pred$elev)] <- 0

# Plot elevation in the input grid
p1 <- ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = elev), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)") + 
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Plot elevation in the prediction grid
p2 <- ggplot(map_pred) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = elev), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)") + 
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

p1 + p2

Figure 3.3: Elevation over Portugal on the input grid (left) and the prediction grid (right), with country boundaries for reference. Country boundaries are overlaid for geographic reference.

3.4 Model

The main objective of this model is to perform spatial disaggregation by increasing the resolution from 0.1\(^\circ\) to 0.02\(^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from 10 km to 2 km using INLA . We assume the existence of a latent continuous spatial process for PM2.5 that is only observed through aggregated measurements, and it is linked to the observations through the aggregation operator in Equation (??). The latent PM2.5 field is then defined as

\[\begin{equation} \text{pm}_{2.5}(\mathbf{s}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{elevation}(\mathbf{s}) + z(\mathbf{s}) + e(\mathbf{s}) \tag{3.1} \end{equation}\]

where \(\beta_0\) is an intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the regression coefficient associated with elevation. The term \(z(\mathbf{s})\) represents a spatially structured random effect, modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process with a Matérn covariance function, and \(e(\mathbf{s})\) is an unstructured error term, modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process that is independent across space.

3.5 Model inputs for INLA

To fit the model described in Equation (3.1), we use the triangulated mesh defined before in Section 3.2. We then construct the SPDE representation on this mesh, and build the corresponding projection matrices that link the observation locations and the prediction points to the mesh nodes. Finally, we combine the response, covariates, and latent components into stacks, which are used to perform model estimation and prediction.

# Construct the SPDE in the spatial mesh
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE)

n.ar <- nrow(map) # number of initial regions
nv <- mesh$n # number of mesh nodes

mesh_sf <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x=mesh$loc[,1],y=mesh$loc[,2],id=1:nv),
                    coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")

# Projection matrix from initial data to the triangulated mesh
A.m <- matrix(0, n.ar, nv)
inter <- as.list(st_contains(map[,c()],mesh_sf))

for (i in 1:n.ar){
  idx <- inter[[i]]
  A.m[i,idx] <- 1/length(idx)
}
A.m <- as(A.m, "dgCMatrix")

# Projection matrix from the mesh to the predicted points
A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = dp)

# Stack for estimation
stk.est <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = df$pm2p5),
  A = list(A.m,1,A.m),
  effects = list(
    s = 1:nv,
    elev = map$elev/1000, # convert m to km 
    b0 = rep(1, nv)
  ),
  tag = "y")

# Stack for prediction
stk.pred <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = NA),
  A = list(A.pr, 1, A.pr),
  effects = list(
    s = 1:nv,
    elev = map_pred$elev/1000, # convert m to km 
    b0 = rep(1, nv)
    ),
  tag = "y.pred")

# Stack for estimation and prediction
stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.est, stk.pred)

3.6 Fitting the model with INLA

Now, we translate Equation (3.1) into an \(\texttt{INLA}\) formula, where the symbol \(\texttt{~}\) defines the linear predictor for the response \(y\). The term \(\texttt{0 + b0}\) adds an explicit intercept, with \(\texttt{b0}\) being a column of ones included in the stack. The term \(\texttt{elev}\) represents elevation as a fixed effect, and \(\texttt{f(s, model = spde)}\) specifies the spatial random effect on the mesh using the SPDE model. We fit the model with \(\texttt{inla()}\) using the stacked data object \(\texttt{stk.full}\), and set \(\texttt{family = "gaussian"}\) because \(y\) is continuous. If the response \(y\) is non Gaussian, such as counts modeled with a Poisson variable, the model specification need to be adapted. For these settings, we recomend using the package inlabru along INLA that provides a workflow to deal with that kind of data (Bachl et al. 2019).

# Time consuming: This preprocessing takes roughly 5 minutes to be executed

# INLA formula
form <- y ~ 0 + b0 + elev + f(s, model = spde) 

# Fitting and prediction 
res <- inla(
  formula=form,
  #verbose = TRUE,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full, spde = spde),
  family = "gaussian",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.full),
                           compute = TRUE, link = 1)
)

# Summary for the fixed effects
res$summary.fixed |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Table 3.1: Table 3.2: Posterior summary of the fixed effects (intercept and elevation coefficient) for the PM2.5 concentration model in Portugal.
mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld
b0 8.399 0.028 8.345 8.399 8.454 8.399 0
elev -0.840 0.092 -1.021 -0.840 -0.660 -0.840 0

Table (3.1) summarizes the posterior distributions of the fixed effects. The posterior mean of the intercept \(\beta_0\) is 8.399~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\), which represents the mean PM2.5 level over Portugal when elevation is zero. The posterior credible interval for the elevation coefficient excludes zero, indicating a clear association between elevation and PM2.5. The posterior mean is \(-0.84\), implying that an increase of 1~km in altitude is associated with a decrease of about 0.84~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) in PM2.5.

3.7 Input data and predicted values

Figure (3.4) compares the coarse input PM2.5 field (left) with the posterior mean predictions from the disaggregation model on the finer grid (right). The disaggregated surface provides a smoother and more detailed representation of spatial variability, while maintaining the main concentration levels and spatial patterns observed in the input data.We also notice that the range of the predicted surface is slightly wider than the range of the input data. This is an important advantage of the disaggregation approach, since it can reveal localized areas with higher or lower concentrations than suggested by the coarse grid, which can be useful for decision makers.

# get indexes of the response variable
idx<- inla.stack.index(stk.full, 'y.pred')$data

# Input grid
map$pm2p5 <- df$pm2p5

# Prediction
map_pred$pm2p5 <- res$summary.linear.predictor[idx, "mean"]

# Plot for input grid
p1 <- ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pm2p5), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pm2.5") + 
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Plot for predictions
p2 <- ggplot(map_pred) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pm2p5), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pm2.5") + 
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Combine plots
p1 + p2

Figure 3.4: PM2.5 over Portugal on the input grid (left) and disaggregated predictions on the finer grid (right).

4 Multivariate Spatial disaggregation of PM2.5, PM10 and Ozone.

In this section, we extend the previous spatial disaggregation framework to a multivariate setting, jointly modeling PM2.5, PM10, and ozone concentrations in Portugal while increasing the spatial resolution from approximately 10 km to 2 km. We use the same CAMS air quality reanalysis data described in Section 3, now incorporating the additional PM10 and ozone fields. The main difference with respect to the univariate case is that the three pollutants are modeled simultaneously, which allows the model to account for their cross dependence and to borrow strength across variables, improving prediction accuracy.

4.1 Data acquisition and preprocessing

To download the data, we follow the same procedure described in Section 3.1. If the code for the univariate spatial example has already been run, there is no need to repeat the registration or licence acceptance steps. The API request remains the same, except that the \(\texttt{variable}\) argument must now include the three pollutants of interest. Specifically, to download PM2.5 PM10, and ozone concentrations for January 2022, we replace the univariate specification with

\[ \texttt{"variable" = ["particulate_matter_2.5um", "particulate_matter_10um", "ozone"]}. \]

All other request arguments are kept unchanged from the univariate case described in Section 3.1. After downloading and unzipping the data, we follow the same preprocessing steps described in Section 3.1. In this case, we have download three \(\texttt{nc}\) files and for each file we applied a cleaning process, of grouping the observation in space by the mean and then restricting the area of observation to Portugal. To keep the workflow easy to reproduce, and following the univariate example, we also provide the resulting preprocessed data as \(\texttt{mult-data.csv}\), which contains the processed PM2.5, PM10, and ozone values in CSV format.

# Define the squared study region and convert to dataframe
sq <- ext(-9.7,-6,36.9,42.3)

# Read the dataset,compute mean value and crop pm2.5 (From source)
r_pm2p5 <- rast("../../../../data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm2p5.l0.2022-01.nc")
r_mean_pm2p5 <- app(r_pm2p5, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq_pm2p5 <- crop(r_mean_pm2p5, sq)

# Read the dataset, compute mean value and crop pm10 (From source)
r_pm10 <- rast("../../../../data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm10.l0.2022-01.nc")
r_mean_pm10 <- app(r_pm10, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq_pm10 <- crop(r_mean_pm10, sq)

# Read the dataset, compute mean and crop Ozone (From source)
r_o3 <- rast("../../../../data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.o3.l0.2022-01.nc")
r_mean_o3 <- app(r_o3, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq_o3 <- crop(r_mean_o3, sq)

# Clean and standardize the data frame
pm2p5 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_pm2p5, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
pm10 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_pm10, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
o3 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_o3, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)

# Merge and organize information
dfm <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = c("x", "y")), list(pm2p5, pm10, o3))
dfm <- dfm[order(dfm$y,dfm$x), ]
names(dfm) <- c("longitude","latitude","pm2p5","pm10","ozone")
write.csv(dfm, "../../../../data/mult-data.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Figure (4.1) displays the spatial distribution of mean PM2.5, PM10, and ozone over Portugal for January 2022 on the original CAMS grid (about 0.1\(^\circ\), roughly 10 km), which is relatively coarse for local-scale interpretation. The maps suggest a positive spatial association between PM2.5 and PM10, with areas of higher PM2.5 generally aligning with higher PM10. In contrast, ozone shows an opposite spatial pattern, indicating a negative spatial association with PM2.5 and PM10, where higher particulate concentrations tend to coincide with lower ozone levels.

# Read dataset from preprocess file 
dfm <- read.csv("../../../../data/mult-data.csv")
 
# Get portugal and Spain borders
boundary <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("Portugal","Spain")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot PM2.5 contamination and boundary countries
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq_pm2p5) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

# Plot PM10 contamination and boundary countries
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq_pm10) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM10") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

# Plot Ozone contamination and boundary countries
p3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq_o3) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Ozone") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

p1+p2+p3

Figure 4.1: Mean PM2.5, PM10 and Ozone concentration in Portugal during January 2022. Country boundaries for Portugal and Spain are overlaid for geographic reference.

4.2 Input grid, spatial mesh, and prediction locations

In this section, we replicate the procedure described in 3.2 for the multivariate dataset \(\texttt{dfm}\). Since the steps depend only on the spatial dimensions of the data, we can reuse the same code to construct the input grid, the spatial mesh, and the prediction locations, as in 3.2. The result spatial mesh, input grid and prediction data result of this step have to looks like in the Figure (3.2).

# Initial squared grid 
map <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(dfm$longitude)),
                               length(unique(dfm$latitude)))))
st_geometry(map) <- "geometry"
st_crs(map) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Spatial mesh 

sq_sf <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(sq))

hexpts <- fm_hexagon_lattice(
  bnd = st_buffer(sq_sf, 0.1), 
  edge_len = 0.05
)

mesh <- fm_mesh_2d(
  loc = hexpts,
  max.edge = 0.1,
  offset = 0.05
)

# prediction points

spf <- 5 # spatial factor
def <- abs(unique(dfm$latitude)[2]-unique(dfm$latitude)[1])/2 

x <- seq(min(dfm$longitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(dfm$longitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(dfm$longitude))*spf)

y <- seq(min(dfm$latitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(dfm$latitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(dfm$latitude))*spf)

dp <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))
dpdfm <- data.frame(dp)
names(dpdfm) <- c("x","y")

dpdfm_sf <- st_as_sf(dpdfm,coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")
dpdfm_sf$id <- 1:nrow(dpdfm)

4.3 Covariates

As in Section 3.3, we use elevation from the EuroDEM product (EuroGeographics and European NMCAs 2023) as a high resolution covariate, and we align its support with both the 0.1\(^\circ\) CAMS input grid and the 0.02\(^\circ\) prediction grid. In the multivariate setting, elevation is included to explain shared altitude related variability across PM2.5, PM10, and ozone, and to improve the explanatory power of the joint disaggregation model over Portugal. For reproducibility and to reduce computation time, we use the same preprocessed raster \(\texttt{eurodemc.tif}\) described in the univariate case, which is already reprojected to EPSG:4326, aggregated, and cropped to the study region. Therefore, if the univariate example has already been run, this preprocessing step does not need to be repeated.

# Time consuming: after preprocessing this part takes around 1 minute to be executed
r_crop <- rast("../../../../data/eurodemc.tif")

map$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map,mean,na.rm = TRUE)$eurodem
map$elev[is.nan(map$elev)] <- 0

map_pred <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(dfm$longitude)),
                               length(unique(dfm$latitude)))*spf))
st_crs(map_pred) <- "EPSG:4326"

map_pred$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map_pred,mean,na.rm = TRUE)$eurodem
map_pred$elev[is.nan(map_pred$elev)] <- 0

4.4 Model

The multivariate disaggregation model, uses the relation between response variable and the information of fine resolution covariates. This model, as the univariate case, assumes the existence of three independent latent continuous spatial process to express the response variable as a linear combination of this processes using the Linear Model of Corregionalization (LMC). Then for a \(M\)-multivariate response variable \(\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{s}) = [W_1(\mathbf{s}), \dots, W_M(\mathbf{s})]^\top\), we can express this using the LCM as \(\mathbf{W}(\textbf{s}) = \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{{U}}(\textbf{s})\) where \(\{\mathbf{U}(\textbf{s})\}\) represents \(M\) independent latent spatial processes and \(\Lambda\) is a \(M\) dimensional squared matrix that defined the multivariate correlation structure between response variables.

For identifiability of the independent processes \(\mathbf{U}(\mathbf{s})\), constraints must be imposed on the coregionalization matrix \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) to avoid rotational aliasing, requiring \(M \times (M-1)\) restrictions. A common choice is to set \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) as a lower triangular matrix with ones on the diagonal (Geweke and Zhou 1996). Under these conditions the response variable \(\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{s})\) could be expresed as

\[\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} W_1(\textbf{s}) \\ W_2(\textbf{s}) \\ \vdots \\ W_M(\textbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \lambda_{21} & 1& \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \lambda_{M1} & \lambda_{M2} & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} U_1(\textbf{s}) \\ U_2(\textbf{s}) \\ \vdots \\ U_M(\textbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} \tag{4.1} \end{equation*}\]

This leads to the following system of equations:

\[\begin{align} \begin{split} W_1(\textbf{s}) & = U_1(\textbf{s}), \\[3mm] W_2(\textbf{s}) & = \lambda_{21} U_1 (\textbf{s}) + U_2(\textbf{s}), \\[3mm] & \hspace{0.2cm} \vdots \\[3mm] W_M(\textbf{s}) & = \lambda_{M1} U_1(\textbf{s}) + \lambda_{M2} (\textbf{s}) + \dots + U_M(\textbf{s}). \end{split} \tag{4.2} \end{align}\]

For the application, the main objective of the multivariate disaggregation model is to disaggregate PM2.5, PM10, and ozone by increasing the spatial resolution from \(0.1^\circ\) to \(0.02^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from \(10\) km to \(2\) km. We adopt the LMC structure defined in Equations (4.1) and (4.2), and include elevation as a covariate. The resulting model is

\[\begin{align} \begin{split} \text{pm}_{2.5}(\mathbf{s}) & = \alpha_1+\beta_1 \cdot \text{elevation} (\mathbf{s}) + z_{1}(\mathbf{s}) + e_1(\mathbf{s}) \\ \text{pm}_{10}(\mathbf{s}) & = \alpha_2 +\beta_2 \cdot \text{elevation} (\mathbf{s}) + \lambda_1 z_{1}(\mathbf{s})+z_2(\mathbf{s})+ e_2(\mathbf{s})\\ \text{ozone}(\mathbf{s}) & = \alpha_3 + \beta_3 \cdot \text{elevation} (\mathbf{s}) + \lambda_2 z_{1}(\mathbf{s})+\lambda_3 z_2(\mathbf{s})+z_3(\mathbf{s}) +e_3(\mathbf{s}) \end{split} \tag{4.3} \end{align}\]

where \(\alpha_1\), \(\alpha_2\), and \(\alpha_3\) are intercepts, and \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\), and \(\beta_3\) are regression coefficients for elevation for PM2.5, PM10, and ozone, respectively. The terms \(z_1(\mathbf{s})\), \(z_2(\mathbf{s})\), and \(z_3(\mathbf{s})\) are spatially structured independent random effects, modeled as zero mean Gaussian processes with a Matérn covariance function. The terms \(e_1(\mathbf{s})\), \(e_2(\mathbf{s})\), and \(e_3(\mathbf{s})\) represent unstructured errors, modeled as zero mean Gaussian noise that is independent across space.

4.5 Model inputs for INLA

For INLA modeling, in addition to the input data, spatial mesh, and prediction points, we require further components for estimation and prediction. These include the SPDE specification, the projection matrices, and the stacks for fitting and prediction. In this section, we describe how these elements are defined for the INLA implementation.

4.5.1 SPDE espeficication and projection matrix

Here we describe how to define the SPDE model on the triangulated mesh and how to construct the projection matrix. This step is similar to the first part of Section (ref?)(sec:mod-inp), but we extend the setup to the multivariate case with three responses. In particular, we define three response objects, \(\texttt{y1}\), \(\texttt{y2}\), and \(\texttt{y3}\), as matrices of dimension \(n_{\mathrm{ar}} \times n_{\mathrm{pp}}\), where \(n_{\mathrm{ar}}\) is the number of observed cells and \(n_{\mathrm{pp}}=3\) is the number of pollutants. Each matrix is filled with \(\texttt{NA}\) values, except for the column corresponding to the pollutant being modeled, which is populated with the observed values. For example, \(\texttt{y1}\) stores PM2.5 in the first column, \(\texttt{y2}\) stores PM10 in the second column, and \(\texttt{y3}\) stores ozone in the third column. This construction matches the multivariate linear predictor used in the stacking and projection steps.

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE)

n.ar <- nrow(map) # number of initial regions
nv <- mesh$n # number of mesh nodes
n.pp <- 3 # number of response variables

mesh_sf <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x=mesh$loc[,1],y=mesh$loc[,2],id=1:nv),
                    coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")

# Projection matrix from initial data to the triangulated mesh
A.m <- matrix(0, n.ar, nv)
inter <- as.list(st_contains(map[,c()],mesh_sf))

for (i in 1:n.ar){
  idx <- inter[[i]]
  A.m[i,idx] <- 1/length(idx)
}
A.m <- as(A.m, "dgCMatrix")

# Projection matrix for prediction locations
A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = dp)

# First response matrix for PM2.5 
y1 <- matrix(NA, nrow = n.ar, ncol = n.pp)
y1[, 1] <- dfm$pm2p5

# First response matrix for PM10
y2 <- matrix(NA, nrow = n.ar, ncol = n.pp)
y2[, 2] <- dfm$pm10

# First response matrix for Ozone
y3 <- matrix(NA, nrow = n.ar, ncol = n.pp)
y3[, 3] <- dfm$ozone

4.5.2 Estimation and prediction stacks

Now we create the stack for estimation. In contrast to the univariate case in Section 3.5, the multivariate model requires separate stacks for each response variable. We therefore build three auxiliary stacks, \(\texttt{stk.y1}\), \(\texttt{stk.y2}\), and \(\texttt{stk.y3}\), corresponding to PM2.5, PM10, and ozone, respectively, following the dependence structure in Equation (@ref\tag{4.2}). Each stack specifies the response vector, the projection matrices \(\texttt{A}\) that link observations to the shared and pollutant specific latent fields, and the corresponding fixed effects, including elevation and an intercept. Finally, we combine these auxiliary stacks into a single estimation object, \(\texttt{stk.est}\), using \(\texttt{inla.stack(stk.y1, stk.y2, stk.y3)}\).

# Create the stack for y1 (PM2.5)
stk.y1 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y1),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    intercept.y1 = rep(1, nv),
    spatial.field.sh = 1:nv,
    elev.1 = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km 
  ),
  tag = "y1")

# Create the stack for y2 (PM10)
stk.y2 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y2),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    intercept.y2 = rep(1, nv),
    sh.copy.y2 = 1:nv,
    spatial.field.y2 = 1:nv,
    elev.2 = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km 
  ),
  tag = "y2")

# Create the stack for y3 (Ozone)
stk.y3 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y3),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    intercept.y3 = rep(1, nv),
    sh.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
    y2.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
    spatial.field.y3 = 1:nv,
    elev.3 = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km 
  ),
  tag = "y3")

stk.est <- inla.stack(stk.y1, stk.y2, stk.y3)

Then we construct the prediction stack on the fine grid. We define three auxiliary prediction stacks, \(\texttt{stk.y1.pred}\), \(\texttt{stk.y2.pred}\), and \(\texttt{stk.y3.pred}\), with responses set to \(\texttt{NA}\) because predictions are required at locations where \(y\) is unobserved. In contrast to the estimation stacks, the projection matrix is now \(\texttt{A.pr}\), which links the prediction locations to the mesh, and elevation is taken from \(\texttt{map_pred}\). We combine the three auxiliary stacks into \(\texttt{stk.pred}\), and then merge estimation and prediction into a single object, \(\texttt{stk.full}\).

# Stack for predicting PM2.5
stk.y1.pred <- inla.stack(tag = "y1.pred",
                         data = list(l = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dp),ncol=n.pp)),
                         A = list(A.pr, A.pr, 1),
                         effects = list(
                           intercept.y1 = rep(1, nv),
                           spatial.field.sh = 1:nv,
                           elev.1 = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km 
                         ))

# Stack for predicting PM10
stk.y2.pred <- inla.stack(tag = "y2.pred",
                         data = list(l = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dp),ncol=n.pp)),
                         A = list(A.pr, A.pr, A.pr, 1),
                         effects = list(
                           intercept.y2 = rep(1, nv),
                           sh.copy.y2 = 1:nv,
                           spatial.field.y2 = 1:nv,
                           elev.2 = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km 
                         ))

# Stack for predicting Ozone
stk.y3.pred <- inla.stack(tag = "y3.pred",
                         data = list(l = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dp),ncol=n.pp)),
                         A = list(A.pr, A.pr, A.pr, A.pr, 1),
                         effects = list(
                           intercept.y3 = rep(1, nv),
                           sh.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
                           y2.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
                           spatial.field.y3 = 1:nv,
                           elev.3 = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km 
                         ))

# stack for prediction
stk.pred <- inla.stack(stk.y1.pred, stk.y2.pred, stk.y3.pred)

# stack for estimation + prediction
stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.est, stk.pred)

4.6 Fitting the multivariate model with INLA

To fit the multivariate model in Equation (4.3), we define the \(\texttt{INLA}\) formula \(\texttt{formMult}\). Compared with the univariate case, the main differences are that we include pollutant specific fixed effects, namely three intercepts, \(\texttt{intercept.y1}\), \(\texttt{intercept.y2}\) and \(\texttt{intercept.y3}\), and three elevation effects, \(\texttt{elev.1}\), \(\texttt{elev.2}\) and \(\texttt{elev.3}\), and we represent cross dependence through shared and copied spatial fields. The term \(\texttt{f(spatial.field.sh, model = spde)}\) defines a shared spatial component, while the clauses \(\texttt{copy = "spatial.field.sh"}\) and \(\texttt{copy = "spatial.field.y2"}\) introduce scaled copies of previously defined fields, with \(\texttt{fixed = FALSE}\) indicating that the scaling parameters are estimated. We then fit the model with \(\texttt{inla()}\) using the combined stack \(\texttt{stk.full}\). Since all three responses are continuous, we set \(\texttt{family = rep("gaussian", 3)}\). Finally, we summarize the fixed effects in a table. For additional details on multivariate modeling in \(\texttt{INLA}\), see (Palmí-Perales, Gómez-Rubio, and Martinez-Beneito 2021).

# Time consuming: This code can  take around 30 minutes to run.
# To monitor progress, uncomment the line `verbose = TRUE` in the `inla()` call.

# INLA formula
formMult <- y ~ 0 + intercept.y1 + intercept.y2 + intercept.y3 +
  elev.1 + elev.2 + elev.3 +
  f(spatial.field.sh, model = spde) +
  f(sh.copy.y2, copy = "spatial.field.sh", fixed = FALSE) +
  f(spatial.field.y2, model = spde) +
  f(sh.copy.y3, copy = "spatial.field.sh", fixed = FALSE) +
  f(y2.copy.y3, copy = "spatial.field.y2", fixed = FALSE) +
  f(spatial.field.y3, model = spde)

# Fitting and prediction 
resM <- inla(
  formula=formMult,
  #verbose = TRUE,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full, spde = spde),
  family = rep("gaussian", 3),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.full),
                           compute = TRUE, link = 1),
  control.compute = list(config=TRUE,return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
)

# Summary of the fixed effects of the model
resM$summary.fixed |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

4.7 Input data and predicted values for multivariate data

After fitting the model, Figure (4.2) shows the three pollutants together, with PM2.5, PM10, and ozone on the coarse CAMS grid in the first row and the corresponding posterior mean predictions on the finer grid in the second row. As in the univariate case, the finer grid predictions shows more local spatial variation, and the predicted values can span a slightly wider range than the coarse inputs, which helps bring out possible hotspots or cleaner areas that are hidden at 0.1\(^\circ\) resolution. The main added value here is that the three pollutants are modeled jointly, so the predictions also use the spatial dependence between pollutants, allowing the model to borrow information across PM2.5, PM10, and ozone and produce a more coherent multivariate disaggregation.

# get indexes of each response variable 
idx.y1 <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, 'y1.pred')$data
idx.y2 <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, 'y2.pred')$data
idx.y3 <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, 'y3.pred')$data

# Input grid
map$pm2p5 <- dfm$pm2p5
map$pm10 <- dfm$pm10
map$ozone <- dfm$ozone

# Prediction
map_pred$pm2p5 <- resM$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y1, "mean"]
map_pred$pm10 <- resM$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y2, "mean"]
map_pred$ozone <- resM$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y3, "mean"]

# Plots
vars <- c("pm2p5", "pm10", "ozone")
labs <- c("PM2.5", "PM10", "Ozone")

plot_list_obs  <- vector("list", length(vars))
plot_list_pred <- vector("list", length(vars))

for (i in seq_along(vars)) {
  plot_list_obs[[i]] <- ggplot(map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[vars[i]]]), color = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = labs[i]) +
    geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
    coord_sf(
      xlim = c(-10, -6),
      ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
      expand = FALSE
    ) +
    ggtitle(paste("Observed", labs[i])) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
      plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
    )

  plot_list_pred[[i]] <- ggplot(map_pred) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[vars[i]]]), color = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = labs[i]) +
    geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
    coord_sf(
      xlim = c(-10, -6),
      ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
      expand = FALSE
    ) +
    ggtitle(paste("Predicted", labs[i])) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
      plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
    )
}

p_obs  <- wrap_plots(plot_list_obs,  ncol = 3)
p_pred <- wrap_plots(plot_list_pred, ncol = 3)

p_obs / p_pred

Figure 4.2: Observed and disaggregated pollutant fields over Portugal. The top row shows the observed mean PM2.5, PM10, and ozone on the coarse CAMS grid, and the bottom row shows the corresponding posterior mean predictions from the multivariate disaggregation model on the finer grid. Country boundaries are overlaid for reference.
